content: Cerebral palsy affects approximately 2.1 out of every 1000 live births and is characterized by a variety of motor impairments and movement disorders. Among these, dystonia is a common movement disorder. Dystonia involves sustained or intermittent involuntary muscle contractions that result in twisting, repetitive movements, and abnormal postures. These involuntary contractions are often painful, distressing, and significantly limit an individual’s ability to perform activities and participate in daily life. Oral medications are typically the first-line treatment for dystonia, and trihexyphenidyl is one such medication frequently used by clinicians to manage dystonia in individuals with cerebral palsy. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of trihexyphenidyl on dystonia in individuals with cerebral palsy, using the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (ICF) framework. This framework assesses outcomes in three domains: impairment, activity, and participation. Additionally, the study aimed to assess the type and frequency of adverse effects associated with trihexyphenidyl use. To gather evidence, a comprehensive search was conducted in May 2017 across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, as well as two trial registries. Reference lists and citations were also reviewed to identify additional studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials comparing oral trihexyphenidyl to placebo in individuals with dystonic cerebral palsy. Participants could be of any age and could have dystonia either in isolation or in combination with other movement disorders such as spasticity, ataxia, chorea, athetosis, or hypotonia. Studies were included regardless of the diagnostic method used for dystonia. The primary outcomes were changes in dystonia and adverse effects, while secondary outcomes included mobility, upper limb function, participation in daily activities, pain, and quality of life. Only one study met the inclusion criteria. This study, conducted in Australia, was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, cross-over trial involving 16 children (10 boys and 6 girls) with predominantly dystonic cerebral palsy. The mean age of participants was 9 years, with a standard deviation of 4.3 years and an age range of 2 to 17 years. The study was assessed to have a low risk of bias across various domains, but the quality of evidence was rated as low according to the GRADE system. The study found no significant difference in dystonia severity between the trihexyphenidyl and placebo groups, as measured by the Barry Albright Dystonia Scale (BADS). The BADS evaluates dystonia in eight body regions on a scale from 0 (none) to 4 (severe), with a total score range of 0 to 32. The treated group had a mean BADS score that was 2.67 points higher (indicating worse dystonia) than the placebo group, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of −2.55 to 7.90. This result was based on low-quality evidence. Trihexyphenidyl was associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, with a risk ratio of 2.54 (95% CI 1.38 to 4.67), based on low-quality evidence. There was no significant difference in upper limb function between the groups, as measured by the Quality of Upper Extremity Skills Test (QUEST). QUEST evaluates 36 items across four domains, with a total score range of 0 to 100. The treated group had a mean score that was 4.62 points lower (indicating worse function) than the placebo group, with a 95% CI of −10.98 to 20.22, based on low-quality evidence. The study provided low-quality evidence suggesting improved participation in daily activities in the trihexyphenidyl group. This was measured using three tools: the Goal Attainment Scale (GAS), the Canadian Occupational Performance Measure (COPM) satisfaction subscale, and the COPM performance subscale. The treated group scored 18.86 points higher on the GAS (95% CI 5.68 to 32.03), 2.91 points higher on the COPM satisfaction subscale (95% CI 1.01 to 4.82), and 2.24 points higher on the COPM performance subscale (95% CI 0.64 to 3.84). These results indicate modest improvements in participation and satisfaction with performance in daily activities. The study did not report on outcomes related to pain or quality of life. In conclusion, there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of trihexyphenidyl for managing dystonia in individuals with cerebral palsy. The available evidence does not support significant improvements in dystonia severity, upper limb function, or participation in daily activities, and there is an increased risk of adverse effects. Larger, randomized, controlled, multicenter trials are needed to better evaluate the efficacy of trihexyphenidyl, particularly with respect to its impact on pain and quality of life.
